findings.text: The first paragraph says plainly what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, so a newcomer can say what it is and why it matters within seconds.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: A link near the top goes straight to the next steps. That section gives a clone command, prerequisites, `./setup.sh` and a one-line command to try (`athena ask "add a changelog"`), so the newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself." / Next steps

findings.text: At Athena's own home URL, the title and nearly all of the page are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets three short paragraphs and must work out that the rest is a demonstration of what Athena produces.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title>; "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: This link speaks to an owner ('your decision'), but a first-time visitor is not one. It is unclear who it is for, and it sits in the header next to the newcomer's next step.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust, but the prerequisites do not mention a Rust toolchain. It also does not say whether `./setup.sh` installs one, so a newcomer may be unsure whether installing will work.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: The try-it step does not say which repository Athena acts on, for example the current directory. It also does not say that it will change files and use a paid model, which a careful newcomer would want to know before pressing Enter.
findings.source: "press Enter to run it on your repository."

findings.text: The Counters section refers to transitions by id before the Transitions section, which defines t1–t12, appears. A reader reading top to bottom meets ids they cannot yet decode.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: Several glossary entries say the term is undefined in the source. That is honest, but it leaves the newcomer with words they cannot fully understand on a page meant to explain them.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a durable record." (similar entries for endpoint, heartbeat, wake, captain call)

findings.text: The transition cards are packed with exceptions and jargon, such as exit codes, harness and pin. They are useful for checking the study but heavy going for a first-time reader.
findings.source: Transitions, e.g. t8: "A ship or scout keeps its recorded harness and needs a note; a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead."

findings.text: The page defines key terms before using them and explains how its citations work. That helps a newcomer follow the firstmate study and see the traceability Athena promises.
findings.source: Words used first; "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it"

findings.text: This section uses internal repository details that mean nothing to a newcomer who has not cloned Athena.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
